name: Banana Cordana Leaf Spot
summary: Pale brown oval spots with a yellow halo that join into large dead patches in wet weather.
symptoms: Pale brown oval spots with a yellow halo, often near the leaf edge
Spots join into large dead patches

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L

name: Healthy Banana
summary: No disease is visible on this banana leaf. Keep watching for panama wilt, sigatoka leaf spot, bunchy top.
fertilizer: General reference: 200 : 60 : 300 g per plant per crop, in splits.
Needs plenty of water. Drip irrigation with mulch can save about 40-50% water.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Banana Pestalotiopsis Leaf Spot
summary: Grey-brown spots on older leaves, usually after injury. Rarely serious if the plantation is kept clean.
symptoms: Grey-brown spots with dark margins, mostly on older leaves
Tiny black dots in the spots

chemical: Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L

prevention: Avoid wounds and keep the plantation clean

name: Banana Sigatoka Leaf Spot
summary: The most important banana leaf disease. It destroys leaf area so bunches fill poorly.
symptoms: Pale yellow streaks that turn into brown spots with grey centres
Large parts of leaves dry; bunches fill poorly

cultural: Cut and burn badly infected leaves
chemical: Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L with mineral oil, as per label, alternated with mancozeb

prevention: Remove infected leaves regularly through the season

name: Banana Bacterial Wilt
summary: A serious bacterial wilt. Leaves yellow and wilt, fruit ripens unevenly and rots. There is no cure.
symptoms: Leaves turn yellow and wilt, starting with the youngest
Yellow bacterial ooze from cut stems; fruit ripens unevenly and rots
conditions: Spread by infected tools, planting material and insects visiting the male flower.

cultural: Clean tools with fire or bleach between plants
Remove the male bud with a forked stick
chemical: No chemical cure

name: Chilli Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frog-eye)
summary: Round 'frog-eye' spots that make leaves yellow and fall, weakening the plant.
symptoms: Round spots with light grey centres and dark brown margins
Leaves yellow and drop

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/L

name: Healthy Chilli
summary: No disease is visible on this chilli leaf. Keep watching for leaf curl, die-back and fruit rot, thrips and mites.
fertilizer: Chilli dislikes both drought and waterlogging. Light, frequent irrigation; drip works well.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Chilli Mites and Thrips (Leaf Curl)
summary: Tiny sucking pests that curl and bronze chilli leaves. Thrips curl leaves upward; mites curl them downward.
symptoms: Leaves curl upward and become boat-shaped (thrips) or downward with a bronze look (mites)
Silvery scratches or tiny moving insects under the leaves

chemical: Mites: a recommended miticide such as spiromesifen 22.9 SC @ 1 ml/L
Thrips: a recommended insecticide such as fipronil 5 SC @ 1.5 ml/L (rotate groups)

prevention: Grow 2-3 border rows of maize or sorghum

name: Chilli Nutrient Deficiency
pathogen: Shortage of nitrogen, magnesium, zinc or other nutrients
summary: Yellowing and poor growth caused by missing nutrients rather than disease.
symptoms: Yellowing between the veins or of whole older leaves
Pale, small new leaves
conditions: Poor or unbalanced soil, leaching rain, or root damage.

cultural: Get a soil test to find the missing nutrient
chemical: Foliar spray of a micronutrient mix as per label; urea 1% if nitrogen is short

fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in splits; correct magnesium (magnesium sulphate) and zinc (zinc sulphate) if deficient
prevention: Fertilize based on a soil test

name: Chilli Powdery Mildew
summary: White powder under the leaves with yellow blotches on top, causing early leaf fall.
symptoms: White powdery patches under leaves and yellow blotches on top
Leaves fall early
conditions: Warm, dry days with humid nights.

chemical: Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L or azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L

name: Cotton Alternaria Leaf Spot
summary: Brown spots with rings that cause early leaf fall, especially on potassium-hungry plants.
symptoms: Small brown spots with concentric rings on leaves
Spots join and leaves drop early
conditions: Warm, humid weather and stressed, potassium-deficient plants.

cultural: Remove infected leaves and crop debris
chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L

fertilizer: Correct potassium deficiency; stressed plants get more spots

name: Cotton Bacterial Blight
summary: Angular leaf spots and black streaks on stems (black arm). Spreads with rain splash and infected seed.
symptoms: Angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown-black
Black streaks on stems and bolls
conditions: Warm, wet weather with wind-driven rain.

chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L
Antibiotic sprays (streptomycin, tetracycline) are banned for farm use in India

name: Cotton Fusarium Wilt
summary: A soil-borne wilt that blocks the plant's water pipes. Once a plant wilts it can't be saved.
symptoms: Leaves yellow and wilt, starting from the lower leaves
Brown streaks inside the stem when cut
conditions: Warm soils, sandy acidic soils and root-knot nematodes.

organic: Apply Trichoderma mixed with farmyard manure to the soil
chemical: No cure once wilted; seed treatment with carbendazim helps prevent it

name: Healthy Cotton
summary: No disease is visible on this cotton leaf. Keep watching for pink bollworm, leaf curl virus (whitefly), bacterial blight.
fertilizer: Flowering and boll formation are critical. Too much water in the vegetative stage causes excess leafy growth.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Cotton Verticillium Wilt
summary: A soil-borne wilt that gives leaves a yellow tiger-stripe pattern before they drop.
symptoms: Yellow patches between the veins that turn brown (tiger-stripe look)
Leaves drop; brown streaks inside the stem
conditions: Cool, moist soil and heavy irrigation.

chemical: No effective chemical cure

name: Groundnut Alternaria Leaf Spot
summary: Brown spots that burn the leaf tips, mostly late in the season.
symptoms: Small brown spots with a yellow halo, often at leaf tips
Leaf tips dry and curl
conditions: Warm, humid weather late in the season.

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L

fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer with gypsum at pegging

name: Healthy Groundnut
summary: No disease is visible on this groundnut leaf. Keep watching for tikka leaf spot, stem rot, leaf miner.
fertilizer: General reference: 20-25 : 40-60 : 30-40 kg/ha + gypsum at pegging.
Pegging and pod development are critical. Keep the soil moist and loose when pegs enter the soil.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Groundnut Rosette
summary: A virus that stunts plants into bushy rosettes with few or no pods. There is no cure.
symptoms: Stunted, bushy plants with small, yellow or mottled leaves
Few or no pods

cultural: Sow early and at close spacing
chemical: No cure; control aphids if numbers are high

name: Groundnut Rust
summary: Orange-brown pustules under the leaves that dry the foliage and cut pod yield.
symptoms: Orange-brown powdery pustules on the underside of leaves
Leaves dry but stay attached

chemical: Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/L or tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 1 ml/L

name: Groundnut Tikka Leaf Spot
summary: Early and late leaf spots that strip plants of leaves before harvest.
symptoms: Round brown to black spots on leaves, early ones with a yellow halo
Heavy leaf fall before harvest

chemical: Carbendazim 12% + mancozeb 63% WP @ 2 g/L or tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 1 ml/L

name: Malabar Spinach Anthracnose
summary: Water-soaked spots that turn tan with dark specks and spoil the leaves for sale.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that turn tan with dark specks

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L

name: Malabar Spinach Bacterial Spot
summary: Small dark angular spots that spread with splashing water.
symptoms: Small dark, water-soaked angular spots

chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 2 g/L
Antibiotic sprays (streptomycin, tetracycline) are banned for farm use in India

name: Malabar Spinach Downy Mildew
summary: Yellow patches on top of the leaf with grey fuzz underneath, in damp, humid weather.
symptoms: Yellow patches on top of leaves with grey fuzz underneath
conditions: Damp, humid weather with wet leaves.

chemical: Metalaxyl + mancozeb, as per label

name: Healthy Malabar Spinach
summary: No disease is visible on this malabar spinach leaf. Keep watching for cercospora leaf spot, leaf-eating caterpillars.
fertilizer: A climbing vine that loves heat and moisture. Give it a trellis, keep the soil moist, and pick leaves often.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Malabar Spinach Pest Damage
pathogen: Leaf-eating caterpillars, beetles and leaf miners
summary: Holes, tunnels or chewed edges from leaf-eating insects.
symptoms: Holes, tunnels or chewed edges on leaves

chemical: Spinosad or another recommended insecticide only if damage is heavy; observe the waiting period before harvest

prevention: Use insect net on small plots

name: Mango Anthracnose
summary: The most common mango disease. It spots leaves, blackens flowers and rots ripening fruit.
symptoms: Dark brown to black irregular spots on leaves
Spots join and leaves dry; black spots on flowers and fruit
conditions: Warm, wet weather, especially during new leaf flushes and flowering.

cultural: Prune and burn diseased twigs and fallen leaves
Open up the canopy for air flow
chemical: Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L at new flush and at flowering

fertilizer: Balanced manure and fertilizer for tree vigour
prevention: Spray before flowering in rainy areas

name: Mango Bacterial Canker
summary: Raised black spots on leaves and cracked cankers on twigs and fruit, spread by rain and wind.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that turn black and raised, with a yellow halo
Cracked cankers on twigs and fruit

chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L sprays
Antibiotic sprays (streptomycin, tetracycline) are banned for farm use in India

name: Mango Leaf-cutting Weevil
summary: A weevil that cuts tender new leaves near the base. Cut leaves fall under the tree with eggs inside.
symptoms: Young tender leaves cut cleanly near the base, as if with scissors
Cut leaves lying under the tree
conditions: New leaf flushes in the rainy season.

cultural: Collect and destroy fallen cut leaves, which hold the eggs
Plough the soil around the tree
chemical: Spray a recommended insecticide on new flushes if damage is heavy

name: Mango Die Back
summary: Twigs dry from the tip downward and branches may ooze gum. Stressed trees are hit hardest.
symptoms: Twigs dry from the tip down; leaves turn brown and roll
Gum oozes from cracks on branches
conditions: Stressed trees, rainy weather and pruning wounds.

cultural: Cut diseased twigs 5-8 cm below the dry part and burn them
Paint cut ends with Bordeaux paste
chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L after pruning

fertilizer: Balanced manure and fertilizer to keep trees vigorous
prevention: Avoid water stress and bark wounds

name: Mango Gall Midge
summary: Tiny flies whose larvae form wart-like galls on leaves and attack flowers.
symptoms: Small raised wart-like galls on leaves
Deformed leaves; galls on flowers cause flower drop

cultural: Remove and destroy galled leaves and shoots
Plough under the tree to expose pupae
chemical: Spray a recommended insecticide at bud burst if galls were heavy last season

name: Healthy Mango
summary: No disease is visible on this mango leaf. Keep watching for powdery mildew, anthracnose, mango hopper.
fertilizer: General reference: About 1 kg N, 0.5 kg P2O5 and 1 kg K2O per year for a 10-year tree, in splits.
Stop irrigation for 2-3 months before flowering to encourage blossoms, then irrigate during fruit development.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Mango Powdery Mildew
summary: White powder on flowers and tiny fruits that makes them drop. Can wipe out a season's fruit set.
symptoms: White powdery coating on young leaves, flowers and tiny fruits
Flowers and young fruits drop
conditions: Cool nights, warm days and cloudy, humid weather at flowering.

organic: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L when panicles emerge
chemical: Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L or propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L

prevention: Spray at the start of flowering in prone areas

name: Mango Sooty Mould
summary: A black coating that grows on the sticky honeydew of hoppers, scales and mealybugs. It blocks light rather than infecting the leaf.
symptoms: Black, soot-like coating on the upper leaf that can be rubbed off
Sap-sucking insects such as hoppers or scales nearby

cultural: Control the sap-sucking insects causing the honeydew
Spray a 2% starch solution; it dries and peels off with the mould
organic: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3-5 ml/L against hoppers and scales
chemical: Spray a recommended insecticide against hoppers if numbers are high

name: Lentil Ascochyta Blight
summary: Tan spots on leaves, stems and pods that can break stems in wet weather.
symptoms: Tan spots with dark borders on leaves, stems and pods
Leaves drop; stems break in severe cases

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/L

name: Healthy Lentil
summary: No disease is visible on this lentil leaf. Keep watching for rust, wilt.
fertilizer: One or two light irrigations, at branching and at pod filling, are usually enough.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Lentil Powdery Mildew
summary: White powder on leaves and stems late in the season.
symptoms: White powder on leaves and stems

chemical: Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L

name: Lentil Rust
summary: Pustules on leaves and stems that dry plants early and shrivel the seed.
symptoms: Yellowish, then brown-black pustules on leaves and stems
Plants dry early

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L at first appearance

name: Money Plant Bacterial Wilt
pathogen: Bacteria such as Ralstonia and Xanthomonas species
summary: A bacterial infection that causes dark, water-soaked patches, yellowing and drooping vines. It spreads quickly in warm, wet conditions and through cuttings and scissors.
symptoms: Dark brown or black water-soaked patches on leaves, often with a yellow halo
Vines droop even though the soil is moist
conditions: Warm temperatures, overwatering, leaves that stay wet, and infected cuttings or tools.

cultural: Cut off and throw away infected leaves and vines; don't compost them
Let the topsoil dry between waterings and water the soil, not the leaves
Wipe scissors with alcohol after every cut
organic: Keep the plant apart from your other plants until new growth is clean
chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 2 g/L as a protective spray on the remaining leaves
Antibiotic sprays (streptomycin, tetracycline) are banned for farm use in India

fertilizer: Stop feeding until the plant recovers, then go back to light monthly feeding
prevention: Take cuttings only from healthy vines
Use a pot with a drainage hole and fresh potting mix

name: Healthy Money Plant
summary: No disease is visible on this money plant leaf. Keep watching for root rot (overwatering), brown, crispy leaf edges, mealybugs.
fertilizer: General reference: Balanced liquid fertilizer once a month in spring and summer.
Most money plant problems come from overwatering, not underwatering.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Money Plant Manganese Toxicity
pathogen: Not an infection: too much manganese in the soil
summary: Too much manganese reaches the plant, usually from acidic, waterlogged potting mix or extra micronutrient fertilizer. Leaves get brown speckles and yellowing.
symptoms: Small brown or black specks on older leaves
Yellowing between the veins and crinkled leaf edges
conditions: Very acidic or waterlogged potting mix, and fertilizers or sprays rich in micronutrients.

cultural: Flush the pot with plenty of clean water to wash out excess salts
Repot into fresh, well-draining potting mix
organic: If the mix is very acidic, stir in a little garden lime or wood ash (check the pH first)
chemical: Stop micronutrient sprays and fertilizers that contain manganese

fertilizer: Use a plain balanced NPK fertilizer without micronutrients until new leaves come out clean
prevention: Avoid overwatering: waterlogged, acidic soil releases more manganese

name: Healthy Onion
summary: No disease is visible on this onion leaf. Keep watching for purple blotch, thrips.
fertilizer: Onion has shallow roots and needs frequent light irrigation during bulb development. Stop irrigation 10-15 days before harvest.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Onion Iris Yellow Spot Virus
pathogen: Iris yellow spot virus, spread by onion thrips
summary: A thrips-spread virus that makes eye-shaped straw-coloured spots and early leaf drying.
symptoms: Straw-coloured, diamond- or eye-shaped spots on leaves and flower stalks
Leaves fall over and dry early
conditions: High thrips numbers in hot, dry weather.

chemical: No cure; control thrips with a recommended insecticide

prevention: Rotate crops and avoid planting next to older onion fields

name: Onion Leaf Blight
summary: Spots that grow into long lesions and burn the leaf tips, cutting bulb size.
symptoms: Small yellow to brown water-soaked spots that grow into long lesions
Leaf tips burn and dry
conditions: Warm, humid weather and long dew periods.

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L with a sticker, or tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 1 ml/L

name: Onion Purple Blotch
summary: Purple lesions with yellow margins that can collapse leaves and seed stalks.
symptoms: Small white sunken spots that become purple lesions with yellow margins
Leaves collapse

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L with a sticker every 10 days

name: Healthy Papaya
summary: No disease is visible on this papaya leaf. Keep watching for ring spot virus, foot rot.
fertilizer: General reference: 200 : 200 : 400 g per plant per year, in splits.
Very sensitive to waterlogging; a few hours of standing water can kill plants. Use raised beds.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Papaya Leaf Curl
summary: A whitefly-spread virus that curls the leaves into cups and stunts the plant. There is no cure.
symptoms: Leaves curl downward and inward into cups, with thickened veins
Stunted plants with few fruits
conditions: High whitefly numbers in warm weather.

organic: Yellow sticky traps and neem oil
chemical: No cure; control whitefly with a recommended insecticide

prevention: Don't grow papaya next to tomato or chilli with leaf curl

name: Papaya Mealybug
summary: White, cottony insects that cover leaves, stems and fruit and cause sooty mould.
symptoms: White cottony masses on leaves, stems and fruit
Yellow, crinkled leaves and black sooty mould

cultural: Prune and burn heavily infested parts
organic: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 5 ml/L with a little soap
Release of the parasitoid Acerophagus papayae where available
chemical: Spray a recommended insecticide on heavy infestations

name: Papaya Mites
summary: Tiny mites that speckle and bronze the leaves in hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Fine yellow speckling and bronzing on leaves
Fine webbing under the leaves

chemical: A recommended miticide such as spiromesifen, as per label

prevention: Check leaf undersides weekly in summer

name: Papaya Mosaic
summary: A virus that mottles and distorts young leaves. There is no cure.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic pattern on young leaves
Small, distorted leaves

cultural: Grow maize as a border crop to intercept aphids
chemical: No cure; manage aphids

name: Papaya Ring Spot
summary: The most destructive papaya disease. Leaves become thin and mottled, and fruit shows dark rings.
symptoms: Mottling and narrow, shoestring-like leaves
Dark green rings on the fruit

cultural: Grow maize as a border crop
chemical: No cure; manage aphids

prevention: Use healthy seedlings and isolate new plantings

name: Radish Black Leaf Spot
summary: Dark spots with rings that dry the leaves.
symptoms: Dark brown to black round spots with rings on leaves

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L

name: Radish Downy Mildew
summary: Yellow patches above and white-grey growth below the leaf in cool, damp weather.
symptoms: Yellow patches on top of leaves, white-grey growth underneath

chemical: Metalaxyl + mancozeb, as per label

name: Radish Flea Beetle
summary: Small jumping beetles that riddle young leaves with tiny holes.
symptoms: Many small round shot holes in leaves

chemical: A recommended insecticide only if seedlings are badly damaged

name: Healthy Radish
summary: No disease is visible on this radish leaf. Keep watching for aphids.
fertilizer: Shallow roots. Water lightly and often; dry soil makes roots pithy and hot.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Radish Mosaic
summary: Mottled, distorted leaves from an aphid-spread virus. There is no cure.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green leaves
Distorted leaves

chemical: No cure; control aphids

name: Rice Bacterial Leaf Blight
summary: One of the most damaging rice diseases in India. Leaves dry from the tip in wavy yellow-white stripes, and early attacks (kresek) can kill young plants.
symptoms: Leaves dry from the tip and edges in wavy yellow-white stripes
Milky drops of bacterial ooze on young lesions in the morning
conditions: Warm, humid, windy and rainy weather, flooding, and heavy nitrogen.

cultural: Drain the field for a few days during severe attack
Apply nitrogen in splits and avoid excess
organic: Pseudomonas fluorescens seed treatment and spray, as per label
chemical: Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L can slow the spread
Antibiotic sprays (streptomycin, tetracycline) are banned for farm use in India

fertilizer: Keep potassium adequate; it reduces blight
prevention: Remove weeds and stubble that carry the bacteria

name: Rice Blast
summary: A fungal disease that attacks leaves, nodes and the panicle neck. Neck blast can cause heavy grain loss.
symptoms: Spindle-shaped spots with grey centres and brown edges on leaves
The panicle neck turns black and the panicle breaks (neck blast)
conditions: Cool nights, long dew periods, high humidity and excess nitrogen.

cultural: Avoid excess nitrogen and apply it in splits
organic: Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma
chemical: Tricyclazole 75 WP @ 0.6 g/L at first symptoms and again at heading
Or azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L (rotate groups)

fertilizer: Hold back the nitrogen top dressing while blast is active; keep potassium adequate
prevention: Treat seed with carbendazim or tricyclazole

name: Rice Brown Spot
summary: A fungal leaf spot that is worst on poorly fed or drought-stressed rice. It also discolours grain.
symptoms: Oval brown spots with grey centres, like sesame seeds, scattered over the leaf
Dark spots on husks and discoloured grain
conditions: Nutrient-poor soils (low potassium, silicon or zinc), water stress and humid weather.

organic: Seed treatment with Trichoderma or Pseudomonas fluorescens
chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L

fertilizer: Apply balanced NPK with potassium and zinc; brown spot is often a sign of poor nutrition
prevention: Keep soil fertility up with organic manure

name: Rice Tungro
pathogen: Rice tungro viruses, spread by green leafhoppers
summary: A virus disease spread by green leafhoppers. Infected plants turn yellow-orange and stay stunted. There is no cure.
symptoms: Yellow to orange leaves, starting from the tip
Stunted plants with fewer tillers
conditions: High green leafhopper numbers and fields planted at different times in the same area.

cultural: Pull out and destroy infected hills early
Plant at the same time as neighbouring fields
chemical: No cure for the virus; control green leafhoppers with a recommended insecticide when numbers are high

fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer; avoid excess nitrogen, which attracts leafhoppers
prevention: Remove ratoons and volunteer rice between seasons

name: Sugarcane Banded Chlorosis
pathogen: Not an infection: low night temperature
summary: Pale bands across the leaves caused by cold nights. The cane usually grows out of it when the weather warms.
symptoms: Pale yellow-white bands running across the leaf blade
Bands appear after cold nights

cultural: No spray is needed; new leaves come out normal as it warms up
A light irrigation before a forecast cold night reduces injury
chemical: No chemical treatment needed

fertilizer: Balanced nutrition helps new leaves grow out healthy
prevention: Plant at the recommended time so young cane escapes cold spells

name: Sugarcane Brown Rust
summary: A rust that forms brown pustules under the leaves and dries them early, reducing cane growth.
symptoms: Long orange-brown to dark brown pustules on the underside of leaves
Leaves turn brown and dry
conditions: Mild temperatures with high humidity and heavy dew.

chemical: Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L at first appearance

name: Sugarcane Brown Spot
summary: Reddish-brown leaf spots that join up and dry the leaves early in humid weather.
symptoms: Small reddish-brown oval spots with a yellow halo on both leaf surfaces
Spots join and leaves dry early

cultural: Strip and burn badly infected lower leaves
chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/L

name: Sugarcane Grassy Shoot
summary: A phytoplasma disease that makes a clump produce many thin, pale, grassy shoots and no usable cane.
symptoms: Many thin, pale or white grassy shoots from one clump
Stunted stalks with no millable cane
conditions: Spread through infected seed cane and leafhoppers.

chemical: No cure; control leafhoppers with a recommended insecticide

fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer keeps healthy clumps vigorous
prevention: Plant seed cane treated with hot water or moist hot air (50-54 °C)
Buy seed from certified, disease-free nurseries

name: Healthy Sugarcane
summary: No disease is visible on this sugarcane leaf. Keep watching for red rot, early shoot borer, grassy shoot.
fertilizer: The grand growth phase needs the most water. Drip irrigation with trash mulching saves a large share of water in sugarcane.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Sugarcane Mosaic
pathogen: Sugarcane mosaic virus and related viruses
summary: A virus disease that causes mosaic streaks on young leaves and can stunt the crop. It travels in seed cane.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic patches or streaks on young leaves
Stunted growth in severe cases
conditions: Spread through infected seed cane and aphids.

chemical: No cure; use virus-free seed cane

prevention: Plant virus-free seed cane and resistant varieties

name: Sugarcane Pokkah Boeng
summary: A fungal disease of the youngest leaves during fast monsoon growth. Tops become twisted and pale; severe cases rot the top.
symptoms: Young top leaves are crinkled, twisted and yellow-white at the base
The top rots in severe cases
conditions: Hot, humid weather following a dry spell, during rapid growth.

cultural: Remove and destroy severely affected tops
chemical: Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/L or copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 2 g/L, 2-3 sprays 10-15 days apart

name: Sugarcane Smut
summary: A smut fungus that grows a long black whip from the top of the cane. Spores spread by wind to nearby clumps.
symptoms: A long black whip grows out of the top of the cane
Thin, grassy stalks with many tillers
conditions: Spread by wind-blown spores and infected setts; worse in ratoon crops.

cultural: Cover the whip with a bag, then cut and burn it before spores spread
chemical: Dip setts in a recommended fungicide (such as propiconazole) before planting

prevention: Grow resistant varieties and plant healthy, treated setts

name: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf
summary: A virus disease that yellows the leaf midrib and can reduce cane yield and sugar.
symptoms: Yellowing of the midrib on the underside of older leaves, spreading into the blade
Leaves dry from the tip; tops look bunched
conditions: Spread through infected seed cane and aphids.

chemical: No cure; manage aphids if numbers are high

name: Healthy Tea
summary: No disease is visible on this tea leaf. Keep watching for blister blight, tea mosquito bug.
fertilizer: General reference: Based on yield and soil test; split through the plucking season.
Needs well-distributed rain; sprinkler irrigation in dry months keeps bushes flushing.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Tea Leaf Blight
pathogen: Colletotrichum and Pestalotiopsis species (brown and grey blight)
summary: Brown patches that start at the leaf edge or tip, often after plucking or hail injury.
symptoms: Brown patches with dark margins starting at the leaf edge or tip
Grey centres with tiny black dots
conditions: Wounds from plucking or hail, and humid weather.

chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 2.5 g/L

name: Tea Red Leaf Spot
summary: Small reddish-brown spots on mature leaves that can cause early leaf fall.
symptoms: Small reddish-brown spots on mature leaves
Spots enlarge and leaves fall early

chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 2.5 g/L

name: Tea Red Scab
pathogen: Often linked to red rust (Cephaleuros) on weak bushes
summary: Orange-red scabby patches on leaves and stems, usually on bushes weakened by poor drainage or nutrition.
symptoms: Orange-red scabby or velvety patches on leaves and stems
Affected shoots die back
conditions: Poor drainage, low potassium and humid weather.

cultural: Improve drainage and nutrition, especially potassium
chemical: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 2.5 g/L

name: Turmeric Aphids
summary: Soft-bodied insects that suck sap from young leaves, leaving them curled and sticky.
symptoms: Colonies of small soft insects on young leaves
Leaves curl and become sticky
conditions: Mild weather and lush new growth.

cultural: Spray a strong jet of water to knock them off
chemical: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.3 ml/L only for heavy infestations

name: Healthy Turmeric
summary: No disease is visible on this turmeric leaf. Keep watching for rhizome rot, leaf blotch.
fertilizer: Needs steady moisture and good drainage. Mulch the beds with leaves after planting.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Turmeric Leaf Blotch
summary: Many small yellowish spots that join and give the leaves a reddish-brown, dried look.
symptoms: Many small yellowish spots on both sides of leaves
Spots join; leaves look reddish-brown and dry

chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L or propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L

name: Turmeric Leaf Spot
summary: Oval brown spots with grey-white centres that dry the leaves.
symptoms: Oval brown spots with grey-white centres on leaves
Spots join and leaves dry

chemical: Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L

name: Black Gram Anthracnose
summary: Dark sunken spots on leaves, stems and pods, worse in wet weather.
symptoms: Dark brown sunken spots with red-brown edges on leaves, stems and pods

chemical: Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L

name: Healthy Black Gram
summary: No disease is visible on this black gram leaf. Keep watching for yellow mosaic virus, leaf crinkle virus.
fertilizer: Sensitive to waterlogging; make drainage channels in the rainy season.
prevention: Inspect plants every week, especially in humid weather.
Keep the field or pot clean of dead leaves and weeds.

name: Black Gram Leaf Crinkle
summary: A seed-borne virus that makes leaves large and crinkled and causes flower drop.
symptoms: Leaves become large, crinkled and puckered
Flowers drop; few pods

chemical: No cure

prevention: Use healthy seed from disease-free fields

name: Black Gram Powdery Mildew
summary: White powder on leaves that dries them early.
symptoms: White powder on the upper leaf surface

chemical: Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L

name: Black Gram Yellow Mosaic
summary: The most serious disease of urad and moong in India. Bright yellow patches and very poor pod set.
symptoms: Bright yellow and green patches on leaves
Small, few pods

chemical: No cure; control whitefly with a recommended insecticide
